Series::amax¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::amax() const -> Series
Series::amax(std::int64_t dim) const -> Series
Series::amax(std::int64_t dim, bool keepdim) const -> Series

What It Does¶

amax() reduces by value and keeps only maxima.

This is the reduction-only companion to max(). That difference is important:

  • amax() is always a reduction

  • max(other) has a second elementwise comparison family that amax() does not have

So amax() is the better choice when the public meaning should stay unambiguous: “take maxima along this reduction lane.”

Overload Map¶

amax()

Reduce the whole Series to one overall maximum.

amax(dim)

Reduce one axis and drop that axis from the result.

amax(dim, keepdim)

Reduce one axis and optionally retain it as size 1.

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t)

The axis to reduce.

  • positive dims count from the front

  • negative dims count from the back

  • the dim must land on a real axis after normalization

Changing dim changes which values compete with each other.

keepdim (bool)

Controls result shape after axis reduction.

  • false: remove the reduced axis

  • true: keep it as size 1

This is mostly a shape-management toggle. The maxima themselves do not change; only how the result can be aligned back against the original shape.

Returns¶

Series A reduced Series containing maxima.

  • amax() returns one scalar value for the whole input

  • amax(dim) returns one maximum per surviving lane

  • keepdim=true preserves the reduced axis as a singleton

Gradient¶

amax() is differentiable almost everywhere, with one important tie rule.

If one value is the unique winner in a reduction lane, it receives the whole incoming sensitivity. If multiple values tie for the maximum, the incoming sensitivity is split evenly across those tied winners.

So for a lane [2, 5, 5], the backward of amax() does not choose one winner arbitrarily. Each 5 receives half of the incoming sensitivity.

Examples¶

Example 1. With no arguments, amax() reduces the whole Series to one overall maximum.

auto values = pluss::make_series({
    {1.0, 7.0, 3.0},
    {4.0, 7.0, 6.0},
});

std::cout << values.amax();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=7

Example 2. amax(0) reduces down columns, so each column produces one winner.

pluss::series::print(std::cout, values.amax(0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[4.0000, 7.0000, 6.0000]

Example 3. keepdim=true preserves the reduced axis as size 1.

std::cout << values.amax(1, true);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,1], strides=[1,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[[7],
  [7]]

The maxima match the row-wise reduction you would expect from dim = 1; the only difference is that the row axis stays present as a singleton.

Example 4. Negative dims count from the back.

std::cout << values.amax(-1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[7, 7]

On a rank-2 Series, -1 means the last axis, so this is the same reduction geometry as amax(1).

Example 5. Tied maxima share the backward sensitivity evenly.

auto amax_grad = pluss::make_series({2.0, 5.0, 5.0});
amax_grad.tracks_slope_(true);
amax_grad.amax().reverse();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, amax_grad.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 0.5000, 0.5000]

The scalar objective here is L = max(2, 5, 5) = 5. Because the last two entries tie for the winning value, the incoming scalar sensitivity 1 is split as 1/2 and 1/2.

Example 6. Out-of-range dims fail through the shared reduction checks.

try {
  std::cout << values.amax(2) << "\n";
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

reduce: dim out of range

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • amax() is reduction-only. If you want elementwise pairwise maxima, use max(other) or maximum().

  • keepdim changes shape only.

  • The tie rule matters in reverse-mode: equal winners share sensitivity.

  • Invalid dims fail; they do not clamp to the nearest valid axis.

  • NaN propagates: a single NaN in a reduction lane makes that lane’s result NaN. Filter it out first if you want the maximum of the finite values.

Summary¶

Use amax() when the goal is “largest value per reduction lane” and nothing else.

  • amax() gives one overall maximum

  • amax(dim) gives one maximum per surviving lane

  • keepdim=true keeps the reduced axis for later broadcasting

  • tied winners split backward sensitivity evenly

See Also¶

  • Series::amin: minimum-value companion.

  • Series::max: broader surface that also includes elementwise pairwise maxima.

  • Series::argmax: positions of maxima instead of maximum values.
